title: A slow, sideways opening
text: Hugo opens a novel called Les Misérables with a contented old bishop and admits that his first details have 'no connection whatever with the real substance' of the story. He is setting a moral standard first. Book One is a measuring stick, held up before anyone else arrives.

title: A good man and a great man
text: The meeting with Napoleon is set in 1804, the year he crowned himself emperor. Myriel's reply turns the hierarchy upside down: the Emperor is merely great, the priest is good, and each may profit from the other. Goodness against greatness: the novel's first scene sets the two side by side.

title: The missing years
text: Myriel married, lived in society, lost his wife in exile and came back a priest. Hugo refuses to explain what changed him. Does the gap make him more believable, or less?

title: Counting beds
text: The Bishop does arithmetic out loud: twenty-six patients in a few cramped rooms, three people in a palace. His charity starts with numbers, not feelings. He treats the mismatch as a simple 'mistake' to be corrected, which makes the exchange sound obvious rather than heroic.

title: Monseigneur Welcome
text: The poor choose his name for him, picking out of his baptismal names the one that means something. 'Bienvenu makes up for the Monseigneur,' he says. A title given from above matters less to him than a name given from below.

title: The budget as portrait
text: Hugo prints the Bishop's household budget line by line, seminaries, prisons, debtors, foundlings, with one thousand livres left for himself. A list of expenses becomes a character sketch. You learn what he values by seeing where the money goes.

title: Preaching by example
text: Instead of scolding a stingy canton, the Bishop tells it about a generous one nearby. Each village hears about its neighbour's virtue. Hugo shows a man who persuades by stories rather than threats, and the method suits his gentleness.

title: A diocese of mountains
text: Digne lies in the Alps of Haute-Provence, poor, steep and nearly roadless in 1815. The Bishop's donkey is not a picturesque detail. It is the only practical way to reach the hundreds of chapels in his charge.

title: The road the fault has travelled
text: 'Examine the road over which the fault has passed.' The Bishop judges a wrong by how a person was brought to it. If the weak and the poor go wrong, he says, the guilt lies with the strong who left them in darkness. Hugo offers it as a measure for every judgement a reader is asked to make.

title: The scaffold
text: The guillotine shakes the serene Bishop more than anything else in these pages. He mutters that death belongs to God alone. Hugo campaigned all his life against the death penalty, and here he lets his gentlest character feel its horror at close range.

title: Wit with a point
text: 'Give them to me,' he says to the marquis who claims to have poor of his own. The Bishop's jokes are short and always land on money and the poor. Hugo keeps him from being a plaster saint by giving him a quick, teasing tongue.

title: The purple cloak
text: He wears a warm cloak even in summer so that nobody sees how worn his cassocks are. It is a small vanity in the service of humility. The detail makes his poverty private, not a show.

title: Compassion as God's name
text: Among the names Scripture gives God, the Bishop's margin note picks Compassion as the most beautiful. In a chapter about rye bread and boiled vegetables, this is the one line of theology, and it explains everything around it.

title: An inventory
text: Hugo walks through the house room by room and stops to count the silver: six forks and spoons, a soup ladle, two massive candlesticks. You can feel the narrator wanting you to know exactly what is in that cupboard, and that its key stays in the lock.

title: A door with no bolt
text: The Bishop has the bolts taken off his street door. A latch anyone can lift is all that closes it. 'One should not ask the name of a man who asks for shelter.' The open door is his whole philosophy made into carpentry.

title: Useful flowers
text: He defends his one flower bed as being as useful as the vegetables, 'more so, perhaps'. For a man who gives nearly everything away, this is a quiet claim that beauty is also a need of the soul.

title: No precaution against one's fellow man
text: The Bishop crosses bandit country without an escort because shepherds and brigands alike need to hear of God. The real robbers, he says, are prejudices and the real murderers are vices. He treats danger as something that lives inside people, not on the road.

title: God, or the Devil?
text: The chest of stolen vestments arrives with no explanation but a note. The curé wavers; the Bishop says 'God!' Hugo leaves the brigand's motive unexplained and even refuses to say where the treasure went, which keeps the episode a parable instead of a neat moral.

title: A philosophy for the rich
text: The senator's materialism, enjoy everything and fear nothing after death, is witty and comfortable. The Bishop's answer is to pretend to admire it and point out that only the rich can afford it. Unbelief, here, is a luxury good, and religion is left to the poor like a cheap substitute dish.

title: Letting the opponent talk
text: Hugo gives the senator a long, lively speech and the Bishop a short reply. He trusts the reader to hear the hollowness in the senator's confidence. Irony does the arguing.

title: A second point of view
text: For the first time we see the Bishop through someone else's eyes: his sister's chatty letter, full of frescoes, genealogy and fear. Her worry makes his calm look braver. A saint described by a nervous sister is easier to believe than one described by a narrator.

title: Two shadows
text: Hugo says the women never interfere when the Bishop acts as a bishop; they simply 'confide him to God'. Their love takes the form of not standing in his way. It is a quiet model of devotion that asks for nothing back.

title: The Convention and 1793
text: The Convention was the assembly that abolished the monarchy and tried Louis XVI in 1792–93. Its members were hated by royalists after 1815. G— did not vote for the king's death, but Digne treats him as nearly a regicide, an outcast in his own valley.

title: The bishop who kneels
text: The Bishop arrives cold and judging and ends on his knees asking the dying man's blessing. The argument over the Revolution is never settled point by point. What changes is the Bishop himself, who discovers a goodness he did not expect in a man he was taught to despise.

title: An argument with two strong sides
text: Hugo lets G— land real blows: the crimes of the monarchy against the crimes of the Terror, the child Louis XVII against Cartouche's brother. He does not make the revolutionary a straw man. The chapter's title calls him an 'unknown light'.

title: The narrator disagrees
text: Hugo openly criticises his own saint: it would have been better if the Bishop had not been a royalist, and to applaud a great man's fall is unworthy. Admitting a flaw makes the portrait more trustworthy and shows that Hugo has his own politics.

title: Napoleon's shadow
text: The Hundred Days were Napoleon's brief return from Elba in 1815, ended at Waterloo. The old guardsman who refuses a cross without the Emperor's face shows how fiercely ordinary men still loved him. The Bishop disapproves of the politics and finds the man a job anyway.

title: The worship of success
text: Hugo attacks the way the world mistakes luck for merit, calling the rich great and the lucky clever. People confuse the stars of heaven with the stars that ducks' feet make in a puddle. The Bishop is lonely because goodness offers no career.

title: Incurable poverty
text: Ambitious young priests avoid the Bishop as if his poverty were catching. Hugo's sarcasm is sharp: a saint is a 'dangerous neighbour'. The joke shows how a church can drift from what it preaches.

title: The garden at night
text: After the women go to bed, the Bishop sits under his stunted fruit trees and looks at the stars, dazzled by God rather than studying him. 'A little garden to walk in, and immensity to dream in.' Hugo pairs the smallest space with the largest one.

title: Love spilling over
text: 'Poor beast! It is not its fault!' he says of an ugly spider, and he sprains an ankle avoiding an ant. Hugo describes his faith as an excess of love. It reaches even creatures nobody else would pity.

title: Gentleness as something earned
text: Hints that the young Myriel was passionate, even violent, make his calm a conquest rather than a temperament. Hugo compares it to a hollow worn by dripping water. Goodness, in this book, can be made slowly.

title: Dressing the wound
text: The universe looks to the Bishop like an immense illness. He does not try to solve it. He tries to bandage it. 'Love each other' is his whole doctrine. Hugo is clear that his hero is not a thinker but a practitioner.

title: A coda before the story
text: This short chapter closes Book One by guarding against a misreading: the Bishop is no mystic or system-builder. Fourteen chapters of portrait end here, and the narrative is about to begin. Hugo wants the Bishop's measure fixed before the trial comes.

title: A man seen from outside
text: For a whole chapter the traveller is only described: his shaved head, his huge stick, his purse. Hugo withholds his inner life and shows him the way Digne sees him. We learn his name only when an innkeeper whispers it as an accusation.

title: Every door
text: Two inns, the prison, a peasant's cottage, even a dog's kennel: the rejections pile up until 'I am not even a dog!' Hugo makes society's verdict physical. Paying money is not enough. A record follows him from door to door.

title: Knock there
text: The old lady's last words point to the one house that has no bolt. The reader already knows that door. Hugo has spent fourteen chapters preparing it, and the rejected man has not.

title: Two scenes at once
text: While Valjean wanders the streets, Madame Magloire relays the gossip about him to the Bishop. The reader knows exactly who 'the vagabond' is, and the household does not. The suspense comes from our knowledge, not theirs.

title: Come in
text: She asks for new locks because Monseigneur says 'come in' to anybody. The knock comes, and he says it again. The chapter is built so that the Bishop's principle is tested at the very moment it is questioned.

title: A name thrown like a challenge
text: Valjean announces himself before anyone asks: his name, his sentence, his yellow passport. He expects rejection and gets ahead of it. The Bishop answers that he already knew his name: 'my brother'.

title: Candlesticks and silver
text: The Bishop remarks that the lamp gives poor light and sends for the two silver candlesticks. Then the full silver is laid, as for any guest. Light and silver come out together, in honour of a convict.

title: 'Sir'
text: What stuns Valjean most is a word: 'sir'. 'You call me sir!' After nineteen years of numbers and insults, courtesy is the shock. Hugo shows dignity being given back in the smallest unit of speech.

title: Tact as a form of love
text: The Bishop talks about Pontarlier's cheese co-operatives and never once mentions the galleys. Baptistine notices that he stops short of a phrase that might wound. Hugo shows charity working through what is left unsaid.

title: The fruitières
text: The cheese-dairies of the Jura were real village co-operatives where poor peasants pooled their milk. The Bishop dwells on them because they offer a man without a past an honest trade and a community. It is advice disguised as small talk.

title: That is God's concern
text: 'How do you know I am not an assassin?' The Bishop's answer refuses fear without denying risk. He has chosen to trust, and he leaves the outcome to God. Hugo makes the line short so that its calm stands out against the convict's laugh.

title: The cupboard by the bed
text: Valjean is led through the Bishop's own bedroom just as Madame Magloire is locking the silver into the cupboard at the head of the bed. Hugo makes sure the guest sees where it goes. The reader feels the tension the household does not.

title: A loaf of bread
text: Nineteen years 'for a pane of glass and a loaf of bread'. Hugo gives the numbers coldly: five years for the theft, fourteen more for escapes. The punishment grows on itself, and hunger, the real cause, appears nowhere in the sentence.

title: Seven heads
text: At Bicêtre Valjean can only say he was a tree-pruner of Faverolles and raises his hand seven times as if touching seven children's heads. The gesture says more than a speech. The family then disappears from his life entirely.

title: A man becomes a number
text: At Toulon he becomes 24,601. Hugo strips Valjean's identity layer by layer: family, place, name. The chapter ends with a question about what happened inside that soul.

title: A court inside one man
text: Valjean puts himself on trial and finds himself guilty, then puts society on trial and finds it more guilty: crushed first by its lack of foresight, then by its pitiless foresight. Then he condemns Providence too. Conscience here works like a courtroom, and its verdict hardens him.

title: Light on one side, darkness on the other
text: Hugo says light entered Valjean's soul from one side and darkness from the other. Learning to read at forty sharpens his mind and his hatred together. Education here is not automatically good; it depends on what it feeds.

title: Jean the Jackscrew
text: Hugo spends real care on Valjean's body: worth four men at the capstan, able to climb a wall's corner with back and heels, nicknamed after holding up a balcony's caryatid. The galleys have made him a formidable body as well as a hardened mind.

title: Is there an incorruptible spark?
text: Hugo asks outright whether misfortune can deform a soul completely, or whether some spark always survives. He does not answer. What would count as evidence either way in the chapters that follow?

title: A prose poem in the middle of a story
text: Hugo stops the narrative for a page of pure image: a man overboard, a ship sailing on, birds singing uselessly overhead. Placed between Valjean's past and his night in the Bishop's house, it tells you how to read that past. He is the drowning man, and society is the ship.

title: Who shall resuscitate it?
text: The chapter ends on a question: who can bring back a soul that has sunk in the social night? Hugo asks it while Valjean lies asleep in the Bishop's house, and leaves it open.

title: Free, but not from the sentence
text: His nineteen years of earnings shrink from a hundred and seventy-one francs to a hundred and nine by deductions he does not understand. At Grasse a master pays him half wages and says 'Beware of the prison.' The State robbed him wholesale; now a private man robs him retail.

title: Then came Digne
text: This short chapter fills the gap between release and arrival and ends by looping back: 'Then came Digne.' Hugo tells the story out of order on purpose. We met the man first as Digne saw him, and only now learn how he got there.

title: A clock and a mind
text: The cathedral clock strikes two, then three, then the quarter. Hugo times Valjean's temptation by the bells so that the reader feels each slow step. Notice the odd intrusion of the convict Brevet's checked suspender, the way the mind snags on trivia under stress.

title: The silver again
text: The thought that drives out all others is the cupboard on the right by the head of the bed. Hugo now pays off his own careful inventory: the ladle alone is worth double what Valjean earned in nineteen years. The arithmetic of poverty makes temptation concrete.

title: A door left ajar
text: Everything Valjean meets on his way is open: the window held by a pin, the low wall, the bedroom door the Bishop has not closed. The Bishop's trust has become the burglar's path.

title: Moonlight on the sleeper
text: A cloud parts and moonlight falls on the Bishop's face as he sleeps. Valjean, standing in shadow with an iron bar, is frightened by this 'luminous old man'. Hugo stages the moment as light against darkness, with the crucifix stretching its arms over both of them.

title: Skull or hand
text: He seems ready either to crush that skull or to kiss that hand. He does neither, and takes the silver. Hugo makes the soul a battlefield where the two possibilities stand side by side, and lets neither fully win yet.

title: The shrieking hinge
text: A rusty hinge screams 'like the trumpet of Judgment', and nothing happens. Hugo uses the noise to make Valjean's terror audible. The silence afterwards is the Bishop's trust again: he sleeps through it.

title: Was the silver ever ours?
text: The Bishop's first response to the theft is to ask whether he had any right to the silver in the first place. It belonged to the poor, and the man was poor. He reframes the crime before the gendarmes even arrive.

title: Mercy that binds
text: 'I gave you the candlesticks too.' The Bishop's lie saves Valjean from the galleys, and his gift adds to the loot. Then he claims a promise Valjean never made and says he has bought his soul for God. This is not leniency. It lays an obligation on the man.

title: So he is not the curé?
text: Valjean learns only now that his host is a bishop, when the brigadier says 'Monseigneur'. Hugo makes the revelation small and dazed. The man of high rank has been playing a humble priest the whole time.

title: The beast acting by habit
text: Valjean steals a child's forty sous almost without knowing it, and then is horrified. Hugo explains that it was the old convict acting from habit, not the man he is becoming. The theft shows him what he must now leave behind.

title: The coin like an open eye
text: After the sun sets Valjean sees the coin shining in the earth and recoils 'as if from an open eye'. An object becomes a witness. His search across the dark plain, shouting 'Little Gervais!', is the first thing he does for someone else.

title: Rise higher or fall lower
text: Hugo spells out the stakes: after the Bishop's pardon, Valjean must either rise higher than the Bishop or sink lower than the convict. There is no middle ground left. The chapter ends not on a resolution but on a glimpse, a man kneeling in the dark before a door.

title: What he did afterwards no one knows
text: Hugo deliberately turns away from Valjean at the most important moment and gives us only a carter's sighting at three in the morning. Why might he refuse to show the conversion directly?

title: A year made of gossip
text: After Valjean's night of crisis, Hugo jumps to Paris and gives us a list: fashions, scandals, songs, a steamboat called a toy, Byron as 'a certain Lord Baron'. The abrupt change of scale is deliberate. Private drama is set against the noise of public life that ignores it.

title: The Restoration
text: In 1817 the Bourbons had been back for two years. Louis XVIII dated his reign from 1795, as if Napoleon had never happened. The fleurs-de-lys painted on hairdressers' shops and the hounding of Bonapartists show a regime trying to erase twenty-five years.

title: No trivial facts
text: Hugo defends his catalogue: there are no small facts in humanity, and the face of a century is made of the faces of its years. It is a theory of history from below, and a defence of the novelist who stops the story to describe a year.

title: Four and four
text: The students come as a set, Tholomyès, Listolier, Fameuil, Blachevelle, and so do their mistresses. Hugo introduces them like a chorus. Only Fantine is singled out: the youngest, still in her first illusions, the only one none of the men addresses as 'thou'.

title: A girl with no name of her own
text: Fantine never knew her parents; a passer-by gave her her name. Hugo notes she had no family name at all. In a book about names, she enters with almost none.

title: An amour for him, a passion for her
text: Hugo puts the imbalance in one phrase. Tholomyès is thirty, rich, balding and amused by everything; Fantine loves for the first and only time. The book's first love story is lopsided from the start.

title: Lost outskirts
text: Hugo notes how much the edges of Paris have changed since 1817. Saint-Cloud, Sèvres and the country inns were Sunday escapes for working Parisians. He writes like someone recording a city that has since vanished.

title: Psyche, not Venus
text: Hugo spends pages on Fantine's beauty, then insists that what sets her apart is her modesty and chaste astonishment. The others wear low necklines openly; her muslin hides and reveals at once. He wants the reader to see her innocence clearly before anything else happens to her.

title: The swing
text: Tholomyès pushes each girl on the swing at Issy and sings a Spanish ballad. Fantine alone will not swing, and Favorite mutters about her airs. A small refusal marks her off from the game the others are playing.

title: Patience
text: Favorite keeps demanding the surprise, and Tholomyès keeps saying 'Patience'. Hugo strings the promise through the whole day so that the reader starts to wonder about it too.

title: The cat that can become a lion
text: Hugo quotes a police chief assuring the King that the people of the faubourgs are harmless, and answers him: given a pike or a gun, the little man of Paris made the 10th of August and Austerlitz. In the middle of a picnic, he reminds the reader that the crowd has a history.

title: A room with a bed
text: The idyll ends in an ugly room with an alcove and a bed, littered with bouquets and the remains of dinner. Hugo marks the time: from five in the morning to half past four in the afternoon. The day is spending itself.

title: Two voices at once
text: Favorite tells Blachevelle she adores him, then whispers to Dahlia that she detests him and loves a poor actor across the street. 'How I lie!' The short scene shows how love talk in this circle is a performance.

title: Grisettes
text: A grisette was a young working woman, often a seamstress, who might keep a student lover. The arrangement was a known feature of Latin Quarter life. It was understood by most parties, as Favorite shows, to be temporary.

title: A speech that says nothing
text: Tholomyès holds forth on puns, wine, women, sugar and marriage. Hugo lets him ramble because the rambling is the portrait: clever, cynical and empty. Notice that he advises everyone to know when to 'effect his own arrest'.

title: She does not even hear me
text: Tholomyès himself sees that Fantine is a dreamer gazing into the blue: 'I am an illusion; but she does not even hear me.' He understands exactly what she feels and is unmoved by it. Then he tries to kiss her and kisses Favorite by mistake.

title: The fallen horse
text: An old mare collapses under a heavy cart outside the window and never rises. Tholomyès makes a joke-poem of it; Fantine alone says 'Poor horse!' Hugo sets a worn-out creature dying of overwork in front of a table of idle diners.

title: The kiss on the brow
text: The surprise begins with a solemn kiss on each girl's forehead and the men filing out with fingers to their lips. The gesture feels like a farewell before anyone has said goodbye. 'Don't be too long,' Fantine murmurs.

title: Respectability
text: The men's letter calls the girls 'the abyss' and themselves virtuous sons returning to duty, to become prefects and fathers. The postscript adds that dinner is paid. Hugo lets the letter condemn its writers in their own polite words.

title: Laughter, then the turn
text: The girls laugh, and Fantine laughs with them. Then, an hour afterwards, alone, she weeps, and in the last line Hugo tells us she has a child. The whole long, sunny Book Three has been leading to this one sentence.

title: The coach that halts
text: While they wait, the girls watch the diligences thunder past, and one stops briefly before galloping off. Hugo shows the departure right in front of them before the letter explains it.

title: One mother meets another
text: Fantine trusts Madame Thénardier because her little girls look happy on a swing. A mother's love for her own children is mistaken for goodness in general. The title invites the comparison.

title: A swing made of a chain
text: The girls swing in the loop of a rusted chain hung under a wrecked cart. It is a charming picture built from heavy iron. Fantine sees only the charm.

title: A voice from inside
text: Madame Thénardier is the face of the bargain, but a man's voice from inside the shop sets the price. Hugo keeps Thénardier offstage and lets money do the talking. The last exchange, about a 'mousetrap', tells you everything Fantine does not hear.

title: An unmarried mother
text: Fantine cannot find work in Paris and dares not be known as an unmarried mother. In 1818 that status could close every respectable door. Leaving the child is the only way she sees to earn a living for them both.

title: The half-class
text: Hugo places the Thénardiers between the bourgeois and the poor, with the vices of both: coarse people who have risen a little, clever people who have sunk. Their wickedness is a social type as well as a personal one.

title: The sign of the Sergeant of Waterloo
text: Thénardier says he was a sergeant in 1815 and painted the inn sign himself to celebrate a feat of arms. The narrator pointedly declines to vouch for it. A man who advertises his own heroism has introduced himself.

title: Names from cheap novels
text: Madame Thénardier names her daughters Éponine and Azelma from the sentimental romances she reads. Hugo calls this mix-up of names, where ploughboys get Arthurs and viscounts get Jacques, one small eddy of the Revolution's levelling. Even naming has become democratic.

title: Under the table
text: Cosette eats from a wooden bowl under the table with the dog and cat. Her fine clothes are pawned and her mother is told she is thriving. To be poor here means first of all to be unprotected.

title: The Lark
text: The village calls her the Lark because she is small, trembling and up before anyone else. Hugo adds that this lark never sings. The nickname is affectionate, and the people who use it do nothing for her.

title: Love that needs a victim
text: Madame Thénardier hates the stranger because she loves her own daughters, and Cosette takes the blows that might fall on them. Hugo makes a mother's love the cause of the cruelty, not a softening of it.

title: A man without a past
text: A stranger arrives in December 1815 with a knapsack and a thorn stick, saves two children from a fire, and so is never asked for his passport. Hugo gives his arrival in a few lines and lets the details sit. The reader may draw their own conclusions; the narrator draws none.

title: Jet and black glass
text: Imitation jet beads and black glass trinkets were cheap ornaments, popular in mourning jewellery. The stranger's two small technical changes cut costs and raised wages at once. Hugo, a believer in progress, likes a hero who improves an industry.

title: Work for anyone willing to be honest
text: Madeleine's factory asks only goodwill of the men, pure morals of the women and honesty of all. Slack seasons and misery vanish from the district. He treats employment itself as charity.

title: Father, Monsieur, Monsieur le Maire
text: The town's name for him rises with his fortunes: Father Madeleine, then Monsieur Madeleine, then Monsieur le Maire. He refuses the cross and the mayoralty before giving in. He is known only by what he has done, and no one asks where he came from.

title: The gossips' theories
text: The town explains him as a fortune-hunter, then an ambitious man, then an adventurer. Hugo lists the guesses with mild contempt. None of them can account for a rich man who keeps refusing honours.

title: Two candlesticks on the mantel
text: Rumour imagines the mayor's room as a hermit's cave of skulls. The real room is plain mahogany and cheap wallpaper, with one thing worth noticing: two antique candlesticks that appear to be silver. Hugo lets the visitors see them and say nothing.

title: No bad plants, only bad cultivators
text: Madeleine shows villagers the uses of the nettle they are uprooting and ends: there are no bad plants or bad men, only bad cultivators. It is the Bishop's road of the fault, put in a farmer's terms.

title: Strength and stealth
text: He lifts horses, frees stuck wheels, shoots perfectly but never at a harmless creature, and forces poor men's doors at night to leave gold behind. Hugo gives his benefactor the skills of a very different kind of man.

title: The happiness of the blind
text: Hugo pauses on a detail the papers left out: the Bishop was blind in his last years and content, with his sister beside him. His meditation on being loved without seeing, hearing a step, feeling a hand, is one of the tenderest passages so far.

title: Mourning without explanation
text: Madeleine appears in full black the day after the notice. Asked if he was the Bishop's cousin, he says he served in the family in his youth. Then he stops every Savoyard chimney-sweep boy, asks his name and gives him money. Hugo offers these facts without comment.

title: Why the Savoyard boys?
text: The mayor asks each little Savoyard his name before giving him money. What could he be looking for? Hugo does not say, and the town does not wonder.

title: The law in human form
text: Javert worships authority and hates rebellion, and files every crime under rebellion. The functionary can never be wrong; the convict can never be redeemed. He has no malice and no vices, only a rule with no exceptions.

title: A dog born among wolves
text: Hugo explains Javert through an animal: the dog born in a litter of wolves. Born in prison to a fortune-teller and a convict, he could attack society or guard it, and chose to guard. His severity grows out of his origins.

title: I think I have him
text: Javert stares after the mayor with a look that says 'I have seen that man somewhere'. He mutters 'I think I have him!' and then goes silent for three days. Hugo builds suspicion without confirming anything, and the chapter ends on 'until one day something happens'.

title: Saving an enemy
text: Fauchelevent hated Madeleine and tried to harm him. Madeleine offers twenty louis for someone to lift the cart, and when nobody moves he crawls under it himself. The act is generous to a man who did nothing to earn it.

title: The sentence that changes the scene
text: Javert says he has known only one man who could lift such a weight, a convict at Toulon. From then on the rescue has two audiences. Madeleine looks at the dying man and at Javert and understands what lifting the cart would tell the inspector. He smiles sadly and does it.

title: The jackscrew
text: The jackscrew is a quarter of an hour away, and the old man has five minutes. Javert's phrase is that he knew one man 'who could take the place of a screw'. In his mouth a man and a tool are interchangeable.

title: I purchase your horse and cart
text: The horse is dead and the cart is wrecked, and Madeleine still 'buys' them for a thousand francs. The polite fiction lets a proud old enemy accept charity without being humiliated. It is the Bishop's tact again, in a businessman's form.

title: A wolf in its master's clothes
text: When Javert first sees Madeleine wearing the mayor's scarf, he shudders like a watchdog that smells a wolf dressed as its master. Hugo returns to the animal image from Javert's introduction. The dog now has to bow to the man he suspects.

title: Fantine comes home
text: The book's two threads meet at the factory door, which Hugo says is like a friend's face to Fantine. She learns a new trade and earns enough to live. The chapter ends on the plainest happiness: 'She is making her living.'

title: The itch of knowing
text: Hugo digresses on idle people who spy on their neighbours at their own expense, purely to know. Madame Victurnien spends thirty-five francs on a trip to Montfermeil. A woman's ruin starts with gossip paid for out of someone else's spite.

title: A public letter-writer
text: Fantine can sign her name but not write, so she pays a public scribe. In a town of her class, her letters pass through a stranger's hands. Illiteracy makes her secret everyone's business.

title: Good because he gave, just because he dismissed
text: Fantine assumes the mayor gave her fifty francs because he is kind and dismissed her because he is just. She does not think to appeal. Her humility makes her accept a verdict nobody gave her a chance to answer.

title: Charity that gives but does not understand
text: The superintendent has 'the charity that gives but not the charity that understands and forgives'. She judges and expels Fantine in perfect good conscience. Hugo shows how virtue without mercy can do the work of cruelty.

title: The art of poverty
text: Old Marguerite teaches Fantine how to live on nothing: no fire in winter, a coverlet turned into a petticoat and back, supper by the light of a neighbour's window. Hugo describes poverty as a skill to be learned. Twelve sous a day earned, ten owed for the child.

title: Her hair
text: With everything else gone, combing her long hair in the morning still gives Fantine a moment of pleasure. Hugo makes a point of it at the end of the chapter. It is the last thing that is wholly hers.

title: Selling herself by pieces
text: First her hair, for ten francs, then two front teeth, for forty, then herself. Each step down is taken for her child, and each is answered by a lie from Montfermeil. Hugo makes the market for a poor woman's body literal, piece by piece.

title: Two stories at once
text: Hugo tells us at once that the petticoat went to Éponine and that Cosette was never ill. The reader knows the letters are lies; Fantine does not. Our knowledge turns her sacrifices into something hard to watch.

title: Hatred aimed at the wrong man
text: Fantine comes to blame Father Madeleine for everything and sings when she passes the factory. Her hatred is understandable and mistaken. Hugo lets the reader see the misdirection, since we know the mayor never knew.

title: Slavery has not left Europe
text: In three hundred words Hugo names Fantine's story: society buying a slave from hunger and cold, a soul for a morsel of bread. Slavery, he says, survives in Europe; it falls on women and is called prostitution. The novel's commentary breaks through the story like a sermon.

title: No bottom
text: Fantine believes she has reached the bottom, and Hugo says that is an error: fate is never exhausted. He places this tiny essay between her fall and the next scene. It makes the reader dread what comes next.

title: Christus nos liberavit
text: The Latin title means 'Christ has freed us'. Hugo uses it bitterly: Christ's law governs civilisation, he says, but does not yet permeate it. A Christian society still sells women.

title: Hats as politics
text: Hugo notes that under the Restoration royalists wore narrow-brimmed hats called morillos and liberals wore wide bolivars. A dandy's costume was a political badge. Bamatabois wears the royalist kind.

title: A Tholomyès in the provinces
text: Hugo says Tholomyès, had he stayed home, would have become one of these idle young men. The link makes Bamatabois a type, not just a villain. The same careless class that abandoned Fantine now torments her in the street.

title: Snow down a bare back
text: Snow forced between bare shoulders is a small, cruel joke for him and a shock for her. Fantine's ball-dress in winter is a working costume, not a choice. Hugo makes the cold itself part of the insult.

title: Two men fight over a woman's life
text: Javert sees a prostitute who attacked a citizen and elector. The mayor sees a woman driven onto the street and says the highest law is conscience. Fantine watches the two men who hold her life argue, and the one she hated turns out to be her rescuer.

title: The spit and the wiping
text: She spits in the mayor's face, and he wipes it away and orders her freed. Hugo lets the insult and the mercy follow without a pause. He does not ask for an apology.

title: Law against law
text: Madeleine wins by citing the code: municipal police matters are the mayor's to judge, and detention without cause is forbidden. Javert bows like a soldier. Mercy here defeats the law by using the law.

title: A comparison that flickers
text: For an instant, Hugo says, a hideous comparison between what this woman is and what this mayor might be passes through Javert's mind. It is the inspector's suspicion surfacing at the worst moment. Hugo shows it and moves on.

title: Two martyrs
text: Fantine wakes to find the mayor praying before the crucifix, to the martyr on high, he says, and adds to himself: for the martyr here below. He sees her suffering as sacred. It is the first time anyone in the book has looked at her that way.

title: A lark becomes a milch cow
text: Thénardier pads his bills with the doctors' fees for his own daughters and keeps Cosette because her mother's protector is rich. Hugo gives him one perfect phrase: the lark is turning into a milch cow. The child is an investment.

title: A letter posted by hand
text: Javert writes to Paris the same night and posts the letter himself. The town assumes he is resigning. Hugo does not say what it contains, and lets the reader worry.

title: Severe with himself
text: Javert asks to be dismissed, not allowed to resign, because he denounced a magistrate wrongly. He has been severe with others all his life and would be a blackguard to spare himself. His rigidity is ugly and also honest; he applies the rule to himself first.

title: The mayor keeps his back turned
text: Through most of Javert's confession, Madeleine stays bent over his papers. When the name 'Jean Valjean' comes, he turns livid; when the real Valjean is said to be found, the paper drops from his hand. Hugo makes us read the scene through small physical reactions.

title: How Jean becomes Champ
text: Jean Mathieu, said in an Auvergne accent, becomes Chan Mathieu, then Champmathieu. The title makes a joke of the slide. An old man is being convicted partly on the sound of a word.

title: False kindness
text: Javert rejects the mayor's offered hand: the kindness that supports a street-walker against a citizen, he says, disorganises society. In his view mercy is a kind of disorder. That is a coherent philosophy, and Hugo lets him state it plainly.

title: A woman who has never lied
text: Hugo introduces Sister Simplice through one trait: she has never told a lie, not even the small social lies everyone allows. To her Satan has two names, Satan and Lying. In a house where the mayor is hiding a woman's sickness from her, that is a strong trait to place at the bedside.

title: A singular tone
text: Madeleine commends Fantine to the sister in a tone she recalls afterwards. He stays an hour instead of half an hour, then studies a road map and pencils figures. Hugo gives us only what witnesses saw, and keeps us outside the mayor's head.

title: Not all of this was known
text: Book VII opens by warning that not all of what follows was known at Montreuil-sur-Mer. Hugo poses as a historian reconstructing events from witnesses. The device lets him move from public facts to private ones.

title: The knocker set down
text: Madeleine lifts the priest's knocker, holds it, and sets it down without knocking. Whatever he wanted to confess or ask, he decides not to. Then he takes the long way home to avoid passing that door again.

title: A detective in a horse-hirer
text: Master Scaufflaire works out the destination from the figures 5, 6 and 8½ left on his mantel: Hesdin, Saint-Pol, Arras. Hugo lets a comic minor character solve the mystery the mayor is trying to keep. The reader knows what is at Arras.

title: Footsteps overhead
text: We see the night only from below: the cashier hears pacing, a cupboard, furniture moved, and sees firelight through a window open in the bitter cold. Hugo then announces that he will tell us what happened in that room. The external view builds pressure for the internal one.

title: A tempest in a skull
text: Every argument for silence is a good one: a whole town depends on him, Fantine and Cosette depend on him, and the man at Arras is a thief anyway. Hugo makes the wrong choice sound like self-sacrifice. 'I am Madeleine, and Madeleine I remain.' Conscience here has to see through its own best reasoning.

title: Two rules that nearly always agree
text: Since Digne he has lived by two rules: to hide his name and to sanctify his life. Usually they agree. Now they collide. The Bishop's candlesticks, the mourning, the questions to the Savoyards were all moments when goodness was chosen over safety.

title: Into the fire
text: He burns the blouse, the knapsack and the thorn cudgel of 1815, and the forty-sou piece glints in the ashes. Then he takes the candlesticks to melt them, and a voice shouts 'Jean Valjean!' He puts them back. The two kinds of object, the convict's relics and the Bishop's gift, cannot be destroyed in the same way.

title: Dante and Gethsemane
text: Hugo asks us to enter this conscience as Dante entered the gate of hell. He ends by comparing Valjean to another man who pushed away a cup in a garden of olive trees, that is, Christ's night in Gethsemane before the Passion. The references say how serious he thinks this ordinary-looking choice is.

title: Paradise and demon, hell and angel
text: 'Remain in paradise and become a demon, or return to hell and become an angel?' The chapter ends with no decision. Which of his arguments for staying silent did you find hardest to dismiss?

title: The dream of the dead town
text: He dreams of an empty village where silent, earth-coloured men stand behind every door, and the first one tells him he has been dead a long time. Hugo says Valjean later wrote the dream down. It turns his inner crisis into an image of a living death, a man among the buried.

title: Lanterns like fallen stars
text: He wakes and takes the tilbury's two red lanterns for stars fallen to earth. The decision he could not make has been made for him by an order he gave the day before. The portress's 'It is five o'clock' sounds like a summons.

title: Providence as an excuse
text: The broken wheel at Hesdin fills him with immense joy: Providence has stopped him, he has honestly done everything, he can turn back. Then a boy fetches an old woman with a cart. Hugo shows how eagerly a conscience accepts any obstacle as permission.

title: A road of hindrances
text: Broken wheel, bad cart, closed road, broken whiffletree, a missed fact about the hour of the trial. Hugo piles up delays so the reader feels the journey as Valjean does, each one a chance to give up. The tension is not whether he arrives but whether he wants to.

title: Another night on the plain
text: Cold and starving, he remembers his other night journey on the plain near Digne eight years before. Hugo links this drive to the night after Petit-Gervais. Both are journeys away from and towards himself.

title: The first lie refused
text: The maid suggests a small white lie: say the mayor is busy with the council. Sister Simplice blushes, weighs the harm the truth might do, and says only that he has gone away. Fantine fills the silence with hope. The truth, told plainly, does more good than the lie would have.

title: A lullaby forgotten for five years
text: Waiting for the mayor, Fantine sings in a whisper an old cradle song she sang to Cosette and had not remembered since. The nun weeps. Hugo lets one song carry all the years of separation.

title: Joy as medicine
text: The doctor finds her pulse stronger and says great joy has been known to halt even advanced disease. Hugo cuts between Arras and the sickroom so that hope in one place hangs on a decision in the other. The reader carries both.

title: A return ticket
text: His first act in Arras is to book a seat on the one o'clock mail back home. The chapter title is wry: on arrival he takes precautions for departure. He still has not decided, and part of him is planning to leave.

title: Ice and fire
text: A lawyer says the case is over, a woman named Limosin convicted for life, and for a moment Valjean thinks he is too late. Then the lights turn out to be for a second case. Hugo uses a mistaken identity of cases to give us a jolt like the one he feels.

title: Writing his name
text: He tears a leaf from his notebook and writes by a street lantern: M. Madeleine, Mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer. The name that has protected him for eight years becomes the key that opens the courtroom door.

title: A reputation as a pass
text: The usher who turned him away now bows to the ground. The President admits him at once because of what Madeleine has done. He crushes the deferential note as though it tasted bitter. Being honoured feels to him like an accusation.

title: The brass door-handle
text: Only a copper knob separates him from the courtroom. It shines at him 'like a terrible star'. He flees down the corridor, stands a quarter of an hour in the dark, and comes back as though someone were leading him. Hugo makes the whole crisis turn on a door handle.

title: Pache's letter
text: He stares at a framed letter by Pache, mayor of Paris in Year II of the Revolution, and cannot read it. One mayor's relic in front of another mayor who is about to lose his office. Hugo leaves the detail unexplained.

title: Shall I become like that again?
text: The man on the bench looks like Valjean as he entered Digne: wild-eyed, in a blouse, full of hatred. Seeing him, Valjean sees what he was. The trial of another man becomes a mirror held up to his own past.

title: A crucifix in the courtroom
text: The scene is his own trial of twenty-seven years ago come back to life, with one difference: a crucifix now hangs above the President. Hugo marks how the Restoration put religion back into the courts. Whether it changed the justice is another question.

title: Satire of the bar
text: The defence lawyer concedes most of the case in pompous provincial rhetoric, and the prosecutor turns those concessions into proof. He even blames the crime on romantic literature, a joke at Hugo's own expense. The machinery of justice runs smoothly toward the wrong result.

title: Is Champmathieu innocent?
text: Nobody saw him climb the wall; he says he found the branch on the ground. Yet he may have taken it. Does it matter, for the choice in front of Valjean, whether the old man is a thief?

title: Defended by his own poverty
text: Champmathieu's rambling speech about M. Baloup and his daughter in the cold wash-house makes the court laugh. It is, in fact, a precise account of how labour wears out the poor. Nobody in the room is listening for that.

title: Famous!
text: As each convict swears he is Jean Valjean, the prisoner mutters 'Good!' and 'Famous!' with growing satisfaction. His comic incomprehension is also helplessness. The more certain the witnesses, the less he can defend himself.

title: A voice behind the judges
text: The chapter ends on three names cried out, Brevet! Chenildieu! Cochepaille!, and twenty voices answering with a fourth: M. Madeleine! Hugo cuts at the instant of recognition, so the reader hears the name before the man speaks.

title: I am Jean Valjean
text: He takes his name back in open court, and with it the galleys. Doing right costs him everything he built. Hugo has made us feel every argument against it, so the plain sentence lands with full weight.

title: The galleys make the convict
text: He tells the court that he went in a stupid peasant and came out a firebrand; kindness saved him as severity had ruined him. It is the argument of the whole volume, put in the mouth of the man it concerns.

title: Proof by memory
text: When the court suggests a doctor, he proves his identity with details only a fellow convict could know: Brevet's checked suspenders, Chenildieu's burn, Cochepaille's tattooed date. The galleys he hid from are his evidence. The hair turned white in an hour is Hugo's outward sign of the night's cost.

title: To be envied
text: He asks the court to pity him, then says that when he thinks of what he nearly did, he counts himself to be envied. What does he think he has gained?

title: The doctor's mirror
text: Sister Simplice hands him the little mirror used to test whether a patient still breathes. He sees his white hair and says only 'Well!' Hugo chooses a mirror meant for the dying.

title: Can they tell a lie?
text: The nun murmurs that they cannot lie to Fantine. He says 'God will inspire us.' Two people committed to truth face a dying woman who believes her child is coming. The chapter ends on her first word: 'And Cosette?'

title: Then and now
text: Two months earlier, by the same bed, her hair was grey and his was brown. Now hers is grey and his is white. Hugo marks how much has happened to him with a single colour.

title: The doctor's evasion
text: The doctor says the child is here but Fantine must be calm before she sees her. It is a medical lie, and Valjean does not contradict it. Hugo shows how quickly an honest silence becomes a kind of deceit.

title: A child singing in the yard
text: A little girl sings outside and Fantine is certain it is Cosette. Then come plans for a garden, butterflies, letters, a white veil for first communion. Hugo lets her build a whole future in a few sentences, which makes the end of the chapter brutal.

title: Look behind you
text: Fantine sees Javert first and can only sign to Valjean to turn around. Hugo ends the chapter on her terror and his turning. It is the third chapter in a row to end on a sudden recognition.

title: A buckle under the ear
text: Javert looks as correct as ever, except that his stock's buckle sits under his left ear instead of at the back. For a man with no wrinkle in his uniform or his duty, this is an earthquake. Hugo shows inner turmoil through one displaced detail.

title: The evil of the good
text: Javert in triumph is a ferocious archangel, a Saint Michael with his heel on crime. Hugo insists there is nothing base in him: probity and duty, wrongly aimed, remain grand even when hideous. He is to be pitied as every ignorant man who triumphs is pitied.

title: 'The Emperor', not 'Bonaparte'
text: The presiding judge is offended that Madeleine said 'the Emperor' rather than 'Bonaparte' when pointing to Cochepaille's tattoo. Under the Restoration the word you chose marked your politics. A slip of vocabulary helps get the warrant signed.

title: Right on every point
text: Javert has a warrant, and he refuses three days' grace because a convict would run. Every step is legal and defensible. The result is a woman dead of shock. Hugo puts the law's correctness and its cost side by side.

title: 'Thou'
text: Javert addresses the mayor as 'thou', the form used to convicts and dogs. Fantine hears it and does not understand. The shift in grammar strips away his title before anyone explains anything.

title: No other name from now on
text: The narrator says he will call him Jean Valjean and nothing else from now on. Javert shouts that there is no Madeleine and no mayor. Narrator and policeman agree on the name for opposite reasons.

title: What did he whisper?
text: Valjean bends and whispers something to the dead woman that no one hears, and Sister Simplice always said she saw a smile come to the lips. Hugo keeps the words secret. What do you imagine he promised?

title: Two hours to forget
text: Within two hours the town has forgotten everything the mayor did. People who found him too good now say they always suspected. Only the old portress, without thinking, hangs his key and sets out his candle. Hugo measures a reputation against a name.

title: Sister Simplice's lie
text: The woman who has never lied tells two lies to Javert, and he believes her because she has never lied. Hugo prays that this lie be counted to her credit in paradise. Conscience here overrules a rule held for a lifetime.

title: The candlesticks go with him
text: He leaves his money for the poor and the trial costs, labels the cudgel tips and the forty-sou piece as evidence, and takes only the Bishop's candlesticks, wrapped in strips of shirt. What he keeps tells you what he believes he owes.

title: Her grave resembled her bed
text: The curé decides a convict and a prostitute deserve no more and gives Fantine the cheapest burial, in the common pit. Hugo ends Volume One on one flat sentence. The book's first volume closes not with the hero but with the poor woman thrown away.

title: A walk instead of a sequel
text: Volume One ended on a pauper's grave and a fugitive on the road to Paris. Volume Two opens with a stroll in Belgium in May 1861, ducks on a pond, a girl weeding. Hugo deliberately leaves the reader hanging and approaches his next subject on foot, the way a tourist would.

title: The name comes last
text: The narrator sees a gate, a hole in the stone, a mound with a lion on it, and only then hears the name: Hougomont. Hugo withholds 'Waterloo' to the end of the chapter, so the reader discovers the battlefield as he did, by accident.

title: The narrator in person
text: 'The person who is telling this story' steps out as a real traveller. Hugo did visit Waterloo in 1861, while finishing the novel in exile. The present-day walk gives the battle a witness who stands in the same fields decades afterwards.

title: The well with no bucket
text: One well in the yard has no bucket because it is full of skeletons; three hundred bodies were thrown in, and legend says voices called from it that night. Hugo makes a domestic object carry the horror. A farm's ordinary things become relics.

title: Ruins as evidence
text: Hugo reads Hougomont like a detective: the patched door, the cut-away stair, the bullet in every apple tree, the burned feet of a wooden Christ. The battle is told through what it left on walls and wood. History, here, is something you can touch.

title: Three francs
text: Three thousand men died in this one enclosure so that a peasant can now offer to explain Waterloo for three francs. Hugo ends on the guide's patter. Great sacrifices shrink into tourism, and the poor make a living from them.

title: A few drops of water
text: Hugo's opening thesis is that the night's rain lost Napoleon the battle: soft ground delayed his guns until half-past eleven and gave Blücher time to arrive. The fate of Europe turns on the weather. History, in this view, is made of accidents.

title: A passer-by on the plain
text: Hugo disclaims any military authority. One scene of his story is connected with the battle, he says, and he judges 'as the populace does'. He presents himself as a bystander with a moral eye, not a strategist.

title: Turning the clock back
text: Waterloo was fought on 18 June 1815. Hugo notes that this is a little before the events of the first part of his book, so the story jumps backwards, to the summer before Valjean reached Digne. He claims 'the storyteller's right' to do so.

title: A battle shaped like a letter
text: Hugo asks the reader to picture a capital A laid on the ground: two roads for legs, a sunken lane for the crossbar, Wellington at the top, Napoleon at the bottom right. It is a teacher's device, and it works. With the A in mind, the movements of the day become easy to picture.

title: The night that bears his form
text: History's pitiless light now throws shadow where people once saw only rays, Hugo says; it is a misfortune for a man to leave behind him a night shaped like himself. Napoleon is drawn in light and darkness at once.

title: Above and below
text: On 18 June Wellington had the good position, above, and Napoleon the bad one, below. Two wrestlers, Hugo says, clutch at every bush and fold of ground. A chance hollow can stop an army. Geography is already a character.

title: Rembrandt, not the map-maker
text: From noon to four the battle becomes a fog of uniforms and noise that no historian can map. Hugo says Rembrandt would paint it better than a draughtsman. He admits the limits of narrative, and then tells us the battle 'came to a point'.
An English officer noted the first cannon shot at thirty-five minutes past eleven. Hugo grounds his argument in that small fact. Napoleon was waiting for a sun that never came to dry the ground.

title: To do like me
text: Asked for orders in case he is killed, Wellington says 'To do like me'. Under his elm he is impassive while his aide falls beside him. Hugo gives the enemy general cold heroism and short, memorable lines.

title: Hidden things
text: Guns hidden in the brushwood, a battalion lying in the tall wheat, embrasures cut into hedges so well that a French engineer saw no obstacle. The English position is full of concealment. When the line draws back behind the crest, Napoleon cries 'The beginning of retreat!' The reader has learned to distrust what can be seen from below.

title: Ninety chances in a hundred
text: Ill and sleepless, Napoleon has never been in better humour: jokes at breakfast, 'Magnificent!' at the deployment, 'four and twenty handsome maids' for his guns. Hugo dwells on his gaiety. Confidence becomes something to watch.

title: The hollow road
text: The chapter ends on a feature invisible from a distance: a sunken lane twelve feet deep along the crest, marked by stone crosses for old accidents. Hugo describes it and says only that on the day of battle it was 'terrible'. He puts it on our map now; from the French side it cannot be seen.

title: They have altered my field
text: To build the Lion Mound, workers carted away the slope of the ground. Wellington, revisiting, complained that they had altered his battlefield. Hugo warns the modern visitor that the land no longer shows what happened.

title: One enormous sentence
text: Hugo lists the morning's setbacks in a single breathless sentence: Hougomont, Bauduin, Foy, the hidden wall, mired guns, shells sinking into mud, Grouchy's delay. Napoleon, he says, never added up the details, only the total. The sentence makes us add them up for him.

title: A shake of the head
text: Napoleon asks his peasant guide Lacoste something in a low voice, and Lacoste shakes his head, 'probably perfidiously'. Hugo does not say what was asked. The great man's plan pauses on a peasant's answer.

title: Treating destiny as an equal
text: Hugo says a man with the Bérésina and Leipzig behind him might have distrusted Waterloo. Is Napoleon's confidence here a sign of genius or of blindness?

title: The ravine fills
text: The cuirassiers burst over the crest shouting 'Vive l'Empereur!' and find the hollow road under their horses' feet. Rank pushes rank in until the ravine is full of living men, and the rest ride over them. 'This began the loss of the battle.'

title: He embarrassed God
text: Could Napoleon have won? Hugo answers no, because of God: his weight in human destiny upset the balance, and the cemeteries had pleaded against him. Waterloo is not a battle but a change of front by the universe. This is history as Providence.

title: Centaurs storming Olympus
text: Hugo makes the charge mythic: giants on colossal horses, two steel serpents climbing through grapeshot. The grandeur is built up so that the fall into the sunken road is all the more sudden and horrible.

title: A piper's arm
text: Amid the slaughter Hugo picks out a Highland piper playing on a drum until a sabre cuts off his arm and his song together. Single images like this keep the mass of numbers human.

title: Blücher, or night
text: Two exhausted armies hold one plateau; nobody can win it. Wellington has no reserves and tells a general to let himself be killed. At five he looks at his watch and murmurs 'Blücher, or night!' Hugo makes rescue a matter of time.

title: The squares
text: Infantry formed in hollow squares, bayonets outward, could resist cavalry if they did not break. The front rank knelt to take the horses on bayonets; the second rank fired. Seven of thirteen English squares were destroyed and the rest held.

title: Two guides
text: A peasant guide may have misled Napoleon; a shepherd boy led Bülow out of the forest by the one route that could bring guns to Plancenoit. Hugo sets the two side by side. The fate of Europe passes through two anonymous country people.

title: A cloud on the horizon
text: At noon Napoleon saw something toward Chapelle-Saint-Lambert. Soult said it was Grouchy; others said trees. It did not move. Hugo makes the Prussian army appear first as an ambiguous smudge, read according to hope.

title: Shouting for the Emperor as they die
text: The Guard advances knowing it will die and cries 'Vive l'Empereur!' Hugo says history records nothing more moving than that agony bursting into acclamation. He admires the men even while his argument is against their cause.

title: The sun of Austerlitz
text: At eight o'clock the clouds part and the setting sun shines on the Guard, the same sun they saw rise at Austerlitz, Napoleon's great victory of 1805. Hugo uses light to close a whole era.

title: Reserved for French bullets
text: Ney begs the English bullets to find him and they do not. Hugo adds that he was reserved for French bullets. Marshal Ney was shot by a French firing squad in December 1815 for having rejoined Napoleon; Hugo's readers knew it.

title: Lions converted into goats
text: The Grand Army dissolves at once on every side, men trampling the living and the dead. 'And who was fleeing in that manner? The Grand Army.' Hugo makes the collapse total to show that something larger than courage was at work.

title: God has passed by
text: Waterloo, Hugo says, is the hinge of the nineteenth century: the great man had to vanish for the great century to arrive. He condemns Blücher's slaughter of fugitives in the same breath. Providence does not excuse cruelty.

title: Walking back alone
text: At nightfall two officers catch hold of a haggard man walking his horse back toward Waterloo: Napoleon, 'the sleepwalker of a shattered dream'. The chapter's last image is the Emperor reduced to one man on foot.

title: The square shrinks
text: At each discharge the last square draws in its four walls and fires back; distant fugitives stop to listen to the thunder growing smaller. Hugo tells the end through sound and shape. When the English guns fall silent out of something like awe, the stage is set for one word.

title: An obscure officer
text: After pages of emperors and dukes, the climax belongs to a man Hugo calls 'an obscure officer named Cambronne'. The book has been arguing for unknown people all along, and here the argument enters the battle.

title: The real victor
text: Hugo crowns Cambronne the winner of Waterloo: not Napoleon, who fled, nor Wellington, who despaired, nor Blücher, who did not fight. To answer the lightning that kills you with scorn is to conquer. The great men shrink and the unknown man looms.

title: Defending a dirty word
text: Hugo knows 'Merde!' will shock his readers and repeats it 'at his own risk'. He calls it Rabelais answering Leonidas, carnival at the end of an epic. Mixing the lowest and the highest is a deliberate principle of his style.

title: Joseph the postman
text: The chapter ends where the Guard died, with Joseph the postman from Nivelles passing at four in the morning, whistling and whipping up his horse. Ordinary life closes over the grave. Hugo returns to the present of his walk.

title: The winning number
text: What is Waterloo? Not a victory, Hugo says, but the winning number in a lottery, a stake won by Europe and paid by France. 'It was not worth putting a lion there.' Chance, not merit, decided it.

title: Calculation against genius
text: Hugo sets the two generals up as opposites: Wellington the Barême, a famous book of tables, of war; Napoleon its Michelangelo. Genius was beaten by calculation. The comparison is partisan and he knows it, but it is also a portrait of two kinds of mind.

title: Glory to the army, not the captain
text: Hugo gives the honour to the English soldiers, Highlanders, Greys and raw recruits, not to their duke, who called them a 'detestable army'. A column, he says, should bear the statue of a people. History belongs to the many.

title: Not glad of Waterloo
text: Some liberals do not hate Waterloo; Hugo does. It was the kings of Europe against France and the Revolution, carrying divine right with them. Yet the restored monarchy was forced to grant a charter and be liberal in spite of itself.

title: Tomorrow has no bad tools
text: Call revolution Progress, and progress Tomorrow, Hugo says: it uses whatever comes to hand, Bonaparte overturning thrones, Louis XVIII signing a charter. 'The slashers had finished, it was the thinkers' turn.' He reads history as moving forward whatever the generals intend.

title: The mounted Robespierre
text: On 18 June 1815, Hugo writes, 'the mounted Robespierre was hurled from his saddle'. He sees Napoleon as the Revolution on horseback, despotic and revolutionary at once. The phrase holds his whole ambivalence.

title: The Restoration's furniture
text: The white flag and cockade, the Arc du Carrousel hiding its Napoleonic victories behind a royal statue, marble over the pauper's grave of Louis XVI, the Holy Alliance. Hugo lists the props of 1815 the way he listed the gossip of 1817 in Book Three. Both catalogues describe the world Valjean and Fantine live in.

title: Go this way, and not that
text: All of it, the throne, the treaties, the caged Emperor, because a shepherd said to a Prussian, 'Go this way, and not that!' Hugo keeps returning to the smallest cause. Then he asks what any of it matters to the Infinite, for whom a grub equals an eagle.

title: You don't know him
text: Told that Napoleon is dead, an old soldier answers: 'You don't know him.' The defeated man grows larger in exile. The kings reign ill at ease with Saint Helena on the horizon.

title: Why the battle was here
text: After seventeen chapters of strategy, Hugo returns 'of necessity' to the field at night. This is the scene of his story he said was connected with Waterloo. The vast digression narrows to two men in the dark of the hollow road.

title: A rescue that is a robbery
text: The prowler takes the officer's ring, cross, watch and purse, and in doing so drags him alive from under the dead. The officer thanks him as his saviour. The great day ends in a small private lie, and Hugo calls it the prowler's 'succour', in quotation marks.

title: Names exchanged
text: 'Thénardier.' 'I shall not forget that name. My name is Pontmercy.' The marauder gives his name and his invented rank of sergeant; the wounded man promises to remember. A name is offered in gratitude for a theft.

title: The rearguard of every army
text: Hugo describes the stragglers who followed armies: sutlers, sham invalids, marauders who stripped corpses and changed sides with the victor. Wellington ordered such men shot, and the dead were robbed anyway. The sutler's cart waiting by the Nivelles road fits the type.

title: A ghost or a gendarme
text: When the hand closes on his coat, the prowler laughs that he prefers a ghost to a gendarme, and digs the man out from curiosity. Why does he bother to save him at all?

title: News from the papers
text: Hugo skips Valjean's capture, trial and sentence and gives us two newspaper clippings instead. The royalist paper and the Paris paper tell it in their own flat styles. We learn the hero's fate secondhand, the way the public did.

title: From 24,601 to 9,430
text: The title is a whole biography: a man becomes a number, a name, a mayor, and a number again. The newspapers call him 'the man known as M. Madeleine'. Every identity he built has been filed away.

title: What he foresaw came true
text: With Madeleine gone, the factory scatters, wages fall and the poor are left with nothing; tax collection costs double within four years. Hugo confirms that the arguments of his night of hesitation were real. Doing right had a price, and the town paid it.

title: Montfermeil coaches
text: The Journal de Paris reports he was retaken boarding a little coach to Montfermeil. The reader knows who lives at Montfermeil. The paper does not.

title: Folklore as cover
text: Hugo opens with a Montfermeil legend about the devil burying treasure and a sorcerer-monk's Latin couplet: dig, and you may find a coin, a stone, a corpse, a phantom, or nothing. The supernatural story lets the villagers explain away something more ordinary.

title: No one knows who has been in the galleys
text: Thénardier shrugs that nobody knows who has been in the galleys or who will be. It is a cynic's remark, and a true one in this book. He then plies Boulatruelle with wine to find a fortune.

title: A small square chest
text: Boulatruelle saw a strong man he knew 'from the galleys' carry something square into the thicket by moonlight and come out with only a pick and shovel. The chapter is placed straight after the report about missing money. What do you make of the timing?

title: The Spanish war of 1823
text: In 1823 France sent an army under the Duc d'Angoulême to restore the absolute King of Spain against Spanish liberals. Hugo calls it a family affair of the Bourbons with little blood and no honour. He says the revolution of 1830 had its germ in it.

title: Shots fired for nothing
text: Hugo counts the useless salute guns of the civilised world, a hundred and fifty thousand shots a day, while the poor starve. It is one of his abrupt swerves from a ship's arrival into a sermon on waste.

title: A rescue seen from the quay
text: The crowd watches a sailor dangle from a footrope and then a white-haired convict run up the rigging like a cat. Hugo tells the whole scene from the onlookers' viewpoint, as he did with the cart in Montreuil. A gust takes the convict's cap and shows his white hair.

title: Pardon for that man
text: The crowd cries 'Pardon for that man!' and old prison sergeants weep. Then he falls between the ships and is not found. The newspaper closes the matter with a number and a name, as the papers closed his trial two chapters earlier.

title: A village and its water
text: Hugo opens Cosette's story with a practical problem: the church end of Montfermeil has only one spring, a quarter of an hour away, and the water-carrier stops at dusk. Geography becomes a child's terror. Notice how the whole book's suffering is built from such small, concrete facts.

title: Under the table again
text: Christmas Eve: carters drink, a roast turns, the Thénardier girls laugh in the next room, and Cosette knits their stockings on the crossbar under the table, a whip on a nail by the chimney. Hugo arranges the room so that warmth and cruelty sit side by side.

title: A mother who loves some of her children
text: From the dark comes the crying of a three-year-old boy whom Madame Thénardier nursed but does not love. Her motherhood stops at her daughters. Hugo adds one more child to the house to show the limits of her love.

title: Two portraits side by side
text: She is huge, bearded and violent; he is small, sickly-looking and polite. Hugo builds them as a pair of opposites, an elephant and a polecat. Everyone thinks the wife is the master, but a word from the frail husband rules her.

title: A trifle exaggerated
text: Thénardier tells customers he saved a wounded general at Waterloo under grapeshot. Hugo says the reader already knows what that prowess was, and may notice he exaggerates 'a trifle'. The inn's sign is built on a robbery retold as heroism.

title: A fly in a spider's web
text: The tavern is a web and Cosette lies trembling in it, ground in a mill and torn with pincers. The wife's method is blows; the husband's is to let her go barefoot in winter. The child says nothing.

title: A child's private prayer
text: Cosette reflects 'with the gloomy air of an old woman' and prays silently that nobody will need water. When the cistern shows only a trickle she stops breathing. Hugo puts us inside an eight-year-old's arithmetic of dread.

title: Mademoiselle Dog-lack-name
text: Madame Thénardier calls her 'that other beast', 'Mademoiselle Dog-lack-name', 'Mam'selle Toad'. Cosette is never addressed by her name in this chapter. In a book where names carry dignity, she is refused one.

title: A bucket she could sit in
text: The empty bucket is bigger than she is; she could have sat in it. Hugo gives the burden a size before she lifts it, so the reader feels the walk ahead.

title: The lady
text: Opposite the tavern door sits a two-foot doll in pink crepe with real hair, which Cosette calls 'the lady'. She measures the abyss between herself and it and decides one must be a queen to own such a thing. The doll is the measure of everything she lacks.

title: Lights with no stars
text: The booths blaze for midnight mass, and Hugo notes there is not a star in the sky. All the light in the chapter is man-made and for others. Cosette steps out of it into the dark with her pail.

title: Forests are apocalypses
text: Hugo describes the dread of a forest at night: grasses like eels, nettles like clawed arms, a red setting planet like a wound. For a child it is worse than fear. Darkness here is pure terror.

title: Counting to ten
text: Paralysed by the night, Cosette counts aloud to ten, over and over, and it brings her back to herself. It is a small, exact detail of how children cope. Hugo trusts it more than any description of courage.

title: The coin in the spring
text: Her apron pocket empties into the water and the fifteen-sou piece sinks without her noticing. Hugo tells us and does not tell her. We carry the dread of what will happen when she reaches home.

title: A hand lifts the weight
text: 'O my God! my God!' At that moment the bucket weighs nothing; an enormous hand has taken the handle. Hugo says there are instincts for all the encounters of life. 'The child is not afraid.' The chapter ends on the first help she has ever received.

title: Back up the same afternoon
text: Hugo leaves Cosette with the stranger and rewinds to that afternoon in Paris to follow the man's day. It is the same backward step he used for Valjean's arrival in Digne. We see the stranger from outside, through what witnesses noticed.

title: The government in a carriage
text: Louis XVIII drove to Choisy almost every day at two, and the poor women of the quarter set their clocks by him. 'That big fellow yonder is the government.' A fat king who could not walk loved to gallop. The stranger hides from the cavalcade.

title: Stones and a zinc band
text: In the forest the stranger finds a heap of white stones, touches the warts on an ash and a band of zinc on a chestnut, and treads the ground to check it has not been dug. Hugo describes the gestures exactly and explains none of them. The chapter's title points back to Boulatruelle.

title: Who is the man in the yellow coat?
text: Poor but scrupulously clean, white-haired but strong in his stride, avoiding a king's carriage and shaking off a policeman, reading a poster for a play called The Two Convicts. Hugo gives many clues and no name. What do you make of him?

title: Questions in the dark
text: The stranger asks short questions and Cosette answers simply: eight years old, no mother, works all day. When she says her name he 'seems to receive an electric shock'. Hugo keeps his face hidden in the dark and shows only that the name means something to him.

title: Other people have mothers
text: 'Other people have mothers. I have none.' She thinks she never had one. A child who has been told nothing about Fantine has filled the gap with nothing at all.

title: A lead sword
text: Her only toy is a little lead sword no longer than her finger, which cuts salad and the heads of flies. Set against Ponine and Zelma's dolls 'full of gold', it says everything about who is loved in that house.

title: A poor man who may be rich
text: The Thénardiers read the stranger's coat and charge him double. Then he pays five francs for stockings, twenty sous for a lost coin, and buys the grandest doll in the village. Their contempt turns to greed and then to hatred. Money is the only language in which they can see him.

title: Now I own your work; play
text: He buys the stockings she is knitting so that she has the right to stop. 'Now I own your work; play, my child.' He frees her by paying for her time, the only thing this household would recognise.

title: Catherine
text: Cosette retreats from the doll 'as if from the sun', asks permission twice, and names it Catherine. Hugo calls the doll the first form of motherhood. Earlier she swaddled a lead sword; now she has something to love.

title: The wooden shoe
text: On the hearth sit the daughters' dainty shoes, each with ten sous from their mother, and in the darkest corner Cosette's muddy sabot, placed there 'with the trust of a child who has never been anything but disappointed'. The stranger puts a gold louis in it. The Christmas custom becomes a quiet act of justice.

title: 'My mother is dead!'
text: Madame Thénardier tells the stranger the mother 'didn't amount to much' and must be dead. Under the table Cosette rocks her sword-baby and sings 'My mother is dead!' Hugo lets the child turn the slander into a lullaby without understanding it.

title: A bill as a character sketch
text: Supper three francs, room ten, candle five, fire four, 'servisse' one. Thénardier's invented bill, with its spelling mistake, is a portrait in numbers. His wife watches him write it 'in religious admiration'.

title: Selling a child
text: The wife would give Cosette away for nothing. The husband suddenly 'adores' her, mentions four hundred francs of medicine and the need for a passport, and then names his price: fifteen hundred francs. The scene is a market, and the stranger refuses to haggle.

title: Mourning clothes
text: The stranger's bundle holds a complete outfit for a girl of seven, all in black. Cosette walks out of Montfermeil in mourning with a pink doll in her arms. Hugo leaves it to the reader to wonder for whom she is in mourning, and how he knew to bring it.

title: Not alone
text: For the first time in the five years she can remember, Cosette feels that she is not alone. She walks gravely, looking at the sky, and feels as if she were beside the good God. Hugo keeps her joy quiet and serious.

title: Is that all?
text: For the first time in their marriage his wife criticises Thénardier, and the greed she stirs sends him running after the pair. The chapter title is a proverb: he who seeks to better himself may make things worse. Comedy and menace run together.

title: Fantine's note
text: Thénardier demands a paper signed by the mother, and the stranger hands him exactly that: Fantine's note ordering Cosette delivered to the bearer. The reader recognises it from Montreuil. Thénardier mutters that the signature is 'fairly well imitated' and lets it go.

title: The accounts recited
text: The stranger reckons Thénardier's dealings to the sou: a hundred and twenty owed, three hundred and three hundred paid, nine months at fifteen francs. Thénardier has been overpaid. The man's exact knowledge is the trap's 'steel jaw', and Thénardier cannot imagine how he has it.

title: A shopkeeper with a taint of the monster
text: Hugo calls Thénardier a double nature: in calm times a respectable tradesman, given the right shock a blackguard. He regrets twice not bringing his gun. What stops him is the size of a cudgel and a look. His wickedness is real, and it is also cowardly.

title: Jean Valjean was not dead
